# Use case 7: comparative methods on phylogenetic networks

Phylogenetic comparative methods (PCMs) typically assume that species
relationships can be represented by a tree. However, reticulate evolutionary
processes such as hybridization and introgression are common across the tree
of life, and species relationships are often better described by
phylogenetic networks, i.e., directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) in which
some nodes (hybrid nodes) have more than one parent
[@solis2016inferring]. Ignoring reticulation can bias estimates of evolutionary
rates and lead to incorrect model selection [@morley2026evaluating], but PCMs
that explicitly model trait evolution on networks are still scarce, with
notable exceptions such as the extension of Brownian motion (BM) models and
phylogenetic regression to networks by @bastide2018phylogenetic.

Here, we will demonstrate how __GraphExperiment__ can be used as the core data
structure for comparative analyses using graphs (instead of trees)
to represent species relationships. We will use data on
*Xiphophorus* fishes (swordtails and platyfishes) from
@bastide2018phylogenetic, which include phylogenetic networks inferred
with SNaQ and two traits [@cui2013phylogenomics]:
the sword index (length of the sword, an extension of the caudal fin
in males, relative to body size) and female preference for a sword.

```{r here}
#| message: false
#| eval: true

library(here)
library(GraphExperiment)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggraph)
library(ComplexHeatmap)
library(patchwork)

# Load helper functions
source(here("code", "phylo_graph_utils.R"))

set.seed(123) # for reproducibility
```

The helper functions used in this chapter (`read_network_dag()`,
`network_vcv()`, `vcv2graph()`, `graph2vcv()`, and `graph_gls()`) are
defined in the file `code/phylo_graph_utils.R`, and their source code is
available in the [Appendices](appendices.qmd#sec-phylo-helpers).

## Data description

The data comprise a file with three time-calibrated networks (with 0, 1, and 3
reticulations) in extended Newick format, and a CSV file with trait data.

```{r}
# Read networks
networks <- readLines(here("data", "xiphophorus_networks_calibrated.tre"))

# Read traits
traits <- read_csv(here("data", "xiphophorus_morphology_Cui_etal_2013.csv"))
head(traits)
```

We will represent species relationships as DAGs using `igraph` objects.
Edges have attributes `length` (branch lengths) and `gamma`
(inheritance probabilities, i.e., the proportion of the genome
inherited from each parent; for tree edges, `gamma` is 1).
The function `read_network_dag()` reads
networks in extended Newick format and returns such DAGs. Here, we will
use the network with 0 reticulations (i.e., a tree) and
the one with 3 reticulations.

```{r}
# Read tree (0 reticulations) and network (3 reticulations) as DAGs
dag_tree <- read_network_dag(networks[1])
dag_net <- read_network_dag(networks[3])

dag_net

# Hybrid nodes are nodes with in-degree > 1
V(dag_net)[degree(dag_net, mode = "in") > 1]

# Hybrid edges (i.e., edges with gamma < 1)
igraph::as_data_frame(dag_net) |> filter(gamma < 1)
```

Let's visualize the network. For that, we will compute node coordinates
from the major tree (i.e., the tree obtained by keeping only
the hybrid edges with the largest inheritance probabilities), with
node positions on the x-axis representing time since the root. Then, we will
add minor hybrid edges on top.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-dpi: 300

# Get major tree by removing minor hybrid edges
dag_major <- delete_edges(dag_net, E(dag_net)[gamma < 0.5])
root <- V(dag_major)[degree(dag_major, mode = "in") == 0]

# Horizontal positions: distance from the root
depth <- distances(dag_major, v = root, mode = "out", weights = E(dag_major)$length)[1, ]

# Vertical positions: tips ordered by depth-first search, and internal nodes
# in the middle of their children (visiting children before parents)
dfs_order <- names(dfs(dag_major, root, mode = "out")$order)
pos <- setNames(rep(NA, vcount(dag_major)), V(dag_major)$name)
pos[V(dag_major)$is_tip] <- rank(match(V(dag_major)$name[V(dag_major)$is_tip], dfs_order))
pos <- Reduce(function(pos, v) {
    if(is.na(pos[v])) pos[v] <- mean(pos[neighbors(dag_major, v, mode = "out")$name])
    pos
}, rev(dfs_order), init = pos)

# Plot network with the coordinates of the major tree
ggraph(dag_net, layout = "manual", x = depth[V(dag_net)$name], y = pos[V(dag_net)$name]) +
    geom_edge_diagonal(aes(filter = gamma == 1), color = "grey50", flipped = TRUE) +
    geom_edge_link(
        aes(filter = gamma < 1, color = gamma),
        arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
        end_cap = circle(1, "mm"), linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    geom_node_text(
        aes(filter = is_tip, label = name), hjust = -0.1,
        size = 3, fontface = "italic"
    ) +
    scale_edge_color_gradient(low = "#fcbba1", high = "firebrick") +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.2))) +
    labs(edge_color = "Inheritance\nprobability (hybrid edges)") +
    theme_graph(base_family = "sans")
```

## Storing species graphs in a `GraphExperiment` object

The trait data will be stored in a matrix with traits in rows and species
in columns. One species (*X. nezahualcoyotl*) is not in the network, so
we will remove it. We will also add a column with clade information
(northern swordtails, southern swordtails, and platyfishes) to `colData`.

```{r}
# Get trait matrix
tips <- V(dag_net)$name[V(dag_net)$is_tip]
trait_mat <- traits |>
    filter(tipnames %in% tips) |>
    column_to_rownames("tipnames") |>
    as.matrix() |>
    t()

trait_mat[, 1:5]

# Create species metadata
northern <- c(
    "Xbirchmanni", "Xcontinens", "Xcortezi", "Xmalinche", "Xmontezumae",
    "Xmultilineatus", "Xnigrensis", "Xpygmaeus"
)
southern <- c(
    "Xalvarezi", "Xclemenciae", "Xhellerii", "Xmayae", "Xmonticolus", "Xsignum"
)
species_md <- data.frame(
    row.names = colnames(trait_mat),
    clade = case_when(
        colnames(trait_mat) %in% northern ~ "Northern swordtails",
        colnames(trait_mat) %in% southern ~ "Southern swordtails",
        TRUE ~ "Platyfishes"
    )
)
```

Nodes of graphs in `colGraphs` must match column names (here, species)
*exactly*. Since our DAGs contain internal nodes
(ancestors) in addition to tips (extant species),
they cannot be stored in the `colGraphs` slot as they are.
Instead, we will store in `colGraphs` the *species-species*
graphs that comparative methods actually use: the variance-covariance
structure expected under BM. In these graphs, nodes are extant species,
edge weights are the covariances between species (i.e., their shared
evolutionary history), and a node attribute (`variance`) stores the
variances (i.e., root-to-tip distances). These are computed with
`network_vcv()`, which implements the recursive algorithm of
@bastide2018phylogenetic on the DAG: nodes are visited
in topological order, and the trait of each hybrid node is the
average of its parents' traits weighted by inheritance probabilities.


::: {.callout-note}
Native support for graphs containing nodes that are not observations
(e.g., internal nodes of phylogenies and phylogenetic networks) is planned for
future versions of __GraphExperiment__. For now, full DAGs can be stored in
the `metadata` slot, as we will do below.
:::

Instead, we will store in `colGraphs` the *species-species*
graphs that comparative methods actually use: the variance-covariance
structure expected under BM. In these graphs, nodes are extant species,
edge weights are the covariances between species (i.e., their shared
evolutionary history), and a node attribute (`variance`) stores the
variances (i.e., root-to-tip distances). These are computed with
`network_vcv()`, which implements the recursive algorithm of
@bastide2018phylogenetic on the DAG: nodes are visited
in topological order, and the trait of each hybrid node is the
average of its parents' traits weighted by inheritance probabilities.

```{r}
# Get variance-covariance matrices under BM
vcv_tree <- network_vcv(dag_tree)
vcv_net <- network_vcv(dag_net)

# Sanity check: for the tree, we get the same as `ape::vcv()`
vcv_ape <- ape::vcv(ape::read.tree(text = networks[1]))
all.equal(vcv_tree, vcv_ape[rownames(vcv_tree), colnames(vcv_tree)])

# Create a `GraphExperiment` object
species <- colnames(trait_mat)
ge <- GraphExperiment(
    assays = list(traits = trait_mat),
    colData = species_md,
    colGraphs = list(
        tree_vcv = vcv2graph(vcv_tree[species, species]),
        network_vcv = vcv2graph(vcv_net[species, species])
    ),
    metadata = list(dag_tree = dag_tree, dag_net = dag_net)
)

ge
```

As node attributes are automatically added to `colData`,
we can easily see that, under a BM model on the network, hybrid species have
smaller variances than expected under a tree. This is because the
trait of a hybrid is a weighted average of its parents' traits.

```{r}
colData(ge) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    mutate(diff = network_vcv__variance - tree_vcv__variance) |>
    arrange(diff) |>
    head()
```

Let's visualize the difference in shared evolutionary history between
species under the network and under the tree.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-dpi: 300

# Get difference between covariance matrices from `colGraphs`
cov_diff <- graph2vcv(colGraph(ge, "network_vcv")) -
    graph2vcv(colGraph(ge, "tree_vcv"))

# Plot heatmap, with species annotated by clade (from `colData`)
clade_colors <- c(
    "Northern swordtails" = "#1b9e77", "Southern swordtails" = "#d95f02",
    "Platyfishes" = "#7570b3"
)
ha <- HeatmapAnnotation(
    Clade = ge$clade, col = list(Clade = clade_colors)
)
Heatmap(
    cov_diff, name = "Covariance\n(network - tree)",
    top_annotation = ha,
    col = circlize::colorRamp2(c(-4, 0, 4), c("steelblue", "white", "firebrick")),
    row_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 8, fontface = "italic"),
    column_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 8, fontface = "italic")
)
```

The heatmap shows that, by accounting for the hybrid origin of northern
swordtails (with genetic contribution from the lineage leading to
*X. xiphidium*; see network plot above), covariances between northern
swordtails and platyfishes increase, while covariances among northern
swordtails decrease.

## Comparative analyses using graphs

Now, we will fit models of trait evolution using the species graphs stored in
`colGraphs`. The function `graph_gls()` takes
a `GraphExperiment` object, the name of a trait (row), and the name of
a graph in `colGraphs`, and fits a phylogenetic generalized least squares (GLS)
model under BM (or under a Pagel's $\lambda$ model, in which covariances
are multiplied by $\lambda$ to measure phylogenetic signal).
Importantly, `graph_gls()` does not care
whether the graph was derived from a tree, a network, or any other source
(e.g., gene-sharing networks, ancestral recombination graphs, etc.);
it only needs a species-species graph.

```{r}
# Fit models for each combination of trait, graph, and model
fits <- expand_grid(
    trait = rownames(ge),
    graph = colGraphNames(ge),
    model = c("BM", "lambda")
) |>
    pmap(\(trait, graph, model) graph_gls(ge, trait, graph, model)) |>
    bind_rows()

fits |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3)))
```

Both traits show strong phylogenetic signal ($\lambda$ estimates at the
upper bound), in line with @bastide2018phylogenetic. For these two traits,
models based on the tree and on the network fit the data similarly well
(differences in AIC < 2), indicating that the inferred reticulations do not
change conclusions about their mode of evolution. Comparisons like this
are straightforward when all candidate species graphs are stored in the
same object. Finally, let's store the best model for each trait in `rowData`,
so that results stay synchronized with the data.

```{r}
# Get best model for each trait and add to `rowData`
best <- fits |>
    group_by(trait) |>
    slice_min(AIC, n = 1) |>
    ungroup()

rowData(ge)$best_graph <- best$graph[match(rownames(ge), best$trait)]
rowData(ge)$best_model <- best$model[match(rownames(ge), best$trait)]
rowData(ge)$lambda <- best$lambda[match(rownames(ge), best$trait)]

rowData(ge)
```

In summary, by storing traits, species metadata, and species graphs in a
single object, __GraphExperiment__ provides a standard data structure for
developing new comparative methods based on graphs.
Developers only need to write functions that take a `GraphExperiment` object
and the name of a graph in `colGraphs` as input, as we did with
`graph_gls()`, and users can easily compare results obtained with
different representations of species relationships (e.g., trees, networks,
gene-sharing networks, or any other species graph).
